---
title: "Day 2: metagenome assembly and binning"
---

::: {.callout-important title="Before you start"}
Do the [Setup](../setup.qmd) first. Then open a terminal and activate the tools of the course:

```bash
cd ~/mag2026/Metagenomics_course
pixi shell
```
:::

In this tutorial you'll learn how to inspect assemble metagenomic data and retrieve draft genomes from assembled metagenomes

We'll use a mock community of 10 bacteria sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq.
In reality the data were simulated using [InSilicoSeq](http://insilicoseq.readthedocs.io).

The 10 bacteria in the dataset were selected from the [Tara Ocean study](http://ocean-microbiome.embl.de/companion.html) that recovered 957 distinct Metagenome-assembled-genomes (or MAGs) that were previsouly unknown! (full list on [figshare](https://figshare.com/articles/TARA-NON-REDUNDANT-MAGs/4902923/1) )

## Getting the Data

```bash
mkdir -p ~/data
cd ~/data
curl -O -J -L https://osf.io/th9z6/download
curl -O -J -L https://osf.io/k6vme/download
chmod -w tara_reads_R*
```

## Quality Control

we'll use FastQC to check the quality of our data, as well as sickle for trimming the bad quality part of the reads.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/results
cd ~/results
ln -s ~/data/tara_reads_* .
fastqc tara_reads_*.fastq.gz
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
What is the average read length? The average quality?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
Compared to single genome sequencing, what graphs differ?
:::


Now we'll trim the reads using sickle

```
sickle pe -f tara_reads_R1.fastq.gz -r tara_reads_R2.fastq.gz -t sanger \
    -o tara_trimmed_R1.fastq -p tara_trimmed_R2.fastq -s /dev/null
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
How many reads were trimmed?
:::

## Assembly

Megahit will be used for the assembly.

```
megahit -1 tara_trimmed_R1.fastq -2 tara_trimmed_R2.fastq -o tara_assembly
```

the resulting assembly can be found under `tara_assembly/final.contigs.fa`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
How many contigs does this assembly contain?
:::

## Binning

First we need to map the reads back against the assembly to get coverage information

```bash
ln -s tara_assembly/final.contigs.fa .
bowtie2-build final.contigs.fa final.contigs
bowtie2 -x final.contigs -1 tara_reads_R1.fastq.gz -2 tara_reads_R2.fastq.gz | \
    samtools view -bS -o tara_to_sort.bam
samtools sort tara_to_sort.bam -o tara.bam
samtools index tara.bam
```

then we run metabat

```bash
runMetaBat.sh -m 1500 final.contigs.fa tara.bam
mv final.contigs.fa.metabat-bins* metabat
```

MetaBAT 2 writes the bins in a folder whose name ends with the date and time of the run. The `mv` command renames it to `metabat`. Each bin is one FASTA file, `bin.1.fa`, `bin.2.fa`, and so on.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
How many bins did we obtain?
:::

## Checking the quality of the bins

A bin is only a *draft* genome. Before using it, we estimate two numbers:

* **completeness**: which part of the genome is in the bin;
* **contamination**: how much of the bin comes from other genomes.

Nobody knows the true genome, so both numbers are **estimates**. They are based on genes that almost every
bacterium has in exactly one copy (single-copy marker genes): a missing marker lowers the completeness, a marker
found twice raises the contamination.

We will use two tools that make this estimate in different ways, and compare them:

* [CheckM](https://github.com/Ecogenomics/CheckM) (version 1) places each bin in a reference tree and counts the marker genes of its lineage;
* [CheckM2](https://github.com/chklovski/CheckM2) predicts the two numbers with machine-learning models trained on many genomes.

Each tool has its own environment and its own reference data.

### CheckM

Open a **second terminal** and activate the CheckM environment:

```bash
cd ~/mag2026/Metagenomics_course
pixi shell -e checkm1
cd ~/results
```

The first time you run `checkm` you have to get its reference data (289 MB; ask your teacher for the drive copy) and tell CheckM where they are:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
cd ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
curl -O https://data.ace.uq.edu.au/public/CheckM_databases/checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
# check the download: the result must be 631012fa598c43fdeb88c619ad282c4d
md5sum checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
tar -xzf checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
rm checkm_data_2015_01_16.tar.gz
checkm data setRoot ~/mag2026/databases/checkm_data
cd ~/results
```

Now run CheckM on the folder of bins (about 5 minutes):

```bash
checkm lineage_wf -t 2 --gplace_max_memory 2G -x fa metabat checkm/
checkm qa checkm/lineage.ms checkm --tab_table -f checkm.tsv
```

::: {.callout-note}
`--gplace_max_memory 2G` limits the memory of the step that places the bins in the reference tree. Without this limit, CheckM needs far more memory than a laptop has and is stopped by the system ("Killed").
:::

The result is the table `checkm.tsv`. Columns 12 and 13 are the completeness and the contamination:

```bash
cut -f1,12,13 checkm.tsv
```

The other columns give the lineage that CheckM chose for the bin, and how many marker genes were found 0, 1, 2 or more times.

### CheckM2

In the same second terminal, leave the CheckM environment and activate the CheckM2 environment:

```bash
exit
pixi shell -e checkm2
cd ~/results
```

The first time, get the CheckM2 database (1.7 GB to download, 2.9 GB on disk; ask your teacher for the drive copy):

```bash
cd ~/mag2026/databases
curl -L -o checkm2_database.tar.gz "https://zenodo.org/records/14897628/files/checkm2_database.tar.gz?download=1"
# check the download: the result must be 07c10655620843b517d0df0c160d911f
md5sum checkm2_database.tar.gz
tar -xzf checkm2_database.tar.gz
rm checkm2_database.tar.gz
cd ~/results
```

Run CheckM2 on the same bins (about 8 minutes):

```bash
checkm2 predict --lowmem --threads 2 -x fa --input metabat --output-directory checkm2 \
    --database_path ~/mag2026/databases/CheckM2_database/uniref100.KO.1.dmnd
```

::: {.callout-note}
`--lowmem` makes CheckM2 use less memory, at the price of a longer run. Without it, CheckM2 does not fit in 6 GB.
:::

The result is the table `checkm2/quality_report.tsv`. Its first three columns are the name of the bin, the completeness and the contamination:

```bash
cut -f1-3 checkm2/quality_report.tsv
```

### Compare the two tools

Put the completeness and contamination of both tools side by side, for example in a spreadsheet or on paper.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
Do CheckM and CheckM2 agree? For which bins do they differ the most?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
The two tools were given exactly the same bins. Why can their estimates differ? Which one is "right"?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
Which bins should we keep for downstream analysis?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If CheckM or CheckM2 does not run on your laptop"}
Tell your teacher. There are two other ways to get the results:

1. **Result files.** The teacher gives you `checkm.tsv` and `quality_report.tsv`, computed on the same data. Use them for the comparison.
2. **Galaxy.** Upload your 10 bin files (`metabat/bin.*.fa`, 20 MB) to [usegalaxy.eu](https://usegalaxy.eu), make a collection of them, and run the tools "CheckM lineage_wf" and "CheckM2" on it.
:::

When you have finished, close the second terminal, or type `exit` to leave the environment.

## Functional annotation

Now we should have a collection of MAGs that we can further analyze. The first step is to predict genes as right now we only have raw genomic sequences. We will use Prokka, a widely used annotation tool for prokaryotic genomes.

Prokka is in its own environment: activate it in a new terminal with `pixi shell -e prokka` (from the course folder).

This tool does gene prediction as well as some decent and useful annotations, and is actually quite easy to run!

Prokka produces a number of output files that all kinds of represent similar things. Mostly variants of FASTA-files, one with the genome again, one with the predicted proteins, one with the genes of the predicted proteins. Also, it renames all the sequences with nicer IDs! Additionally, a very useful file generated is a GFF-file, which gives more information about the annotations than just the names you can see in the FASTA-files.

### eggNOG-mapper (on Galaxy)

The annotations of Prokka are good but not very complete for environmental bacteria.
[eggNOG-mapper](https://github.com/eggnogdb/eggnog-mapper) compares each protein with the eggNOG database of
groups of related genes (orthologous groups), and transfers their annotation: gene names, functional categories
(COG), pathways (KEGG) and more. This is a bit heavier in computation.

The eggNOG database takes more than 40 GB, too much for a laptop. So this step runs on **Galaxy**, not on your computer.

1. Choose **one** MAG (don't be greedy, it is not fast!). You need its protein file: the `.faa` file that Prokka made for this MAG.
2. Log in to [usegalaxy.eu](https://usegalaxy.eu) and upload the `.faa` file with the "Upload" button.
3. Search the tool panel for "eggNOG Mapper" and run the tool on your file. Keep the default settings.
4. Wait until the job is green, then open the annotation table.

usegalaxy.eu runs eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13 with version 5.0.2 of the eggNOG database. Write these two versions down: they are part of your result.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
OPTIONAL: understand the output. Find three proteins that Prokka named "hypothetical protein". What does eggNOG-mapper say about them?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If Galaxy is slow or not available"}
The authors of eggNOG-mapper offer a web service: <https://eggnog-mapper.cgmlab.org> (the old address, eggnog-mapper.embl.de, sends you there).
Upload the same `.faa` file and follow the instructions of the page. Submit your job early: jobs wait in a queue, and a job can take an hour or more.
The web service uses a newer database (eggNOG 7), so some annotations differ from the Galaxy result.
:::

## Taxonomic annotation

We now know more about the genes your MAG contains, however we do not really know who we have?! checkm might have given us an indication but it is only approximative.

Taxonomic classification for full genomes is not always easy for MAGs, often the 16S gene is missing as it assembles badly, and which other genes to use to for taxonomy is not always evident. Typically marker genes, min-hashes or k-mer databases are used as reference. It is often problematic for environmental data as the databases are not biased into our direction! We will use a min-hash database of the GTDB representative genomes with a tool called [sourmash](https://sourmash.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).

[GTDB](https://gtdb.ecogenomic.org) is a taxonomy built from genomes. It contains one representative genome per species, including many species known only from MAGs.
sourmash keeps a small "sketch" of each genome: a sample of its k-mers. Comparing two sketches is very fast.

### Get the database

The database of this tutorial is a reduced copy of the sourmash database "GTDB R226, species representatives, k=31", made for this course so that it fits in the memory of a laptop. Your teacher gives you the two files on a drive:

* `gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip` (447 MB): the sketches of the 143,384 GTDB representative genomes;
* `gtdb-rs226.lineages.csv` (103 MB): the taxonomy of each genome.

Copy them into `~/mag2026/databases/sourmash/`. The [Data page](../data/README.md) explains how the reduced file was made and how to rebuild it.

```bash
SOURMASH_DB=~/mag2026/databases/sourmash
ls $SOURMASH_DB
```

### Sketch the bins and search the database

sourmash is in the main environment (the first terminal). For each bin we make a sketch (`sourmash sketch`), then search the genomes of the database that best explain it (`sourmash gather`). This takes about 1 minute per bin.

```bash
cd ~/results
mkdir -p sourmash
for i in metabat/bin.*.fa
do
    name=$(basename $i .fa)
    echo $name
    sourmash sketch dna -p k=31,scaled=10000 --name $name $i -o sourmash/${name}.sig
    sourmash gather sourmash/${name}.sig $SOURMASH_DB/gtdb-reps-rs226-k31.s10k.zip \
        -o sourmash/${name}.gather.csv
done
```

For each bin, `gather` prints the genomes it found and which part of the bin they explain. If nothing in the database is similar enough, it prints "No matches" and writes no file.

### From genomes to a taxonomy

`sourmash tax genome` reads the matches and the taxonomy file, and gives one classification per bin:

```bash
sourmash tax genome -g sourmash/*.gather.csv -t $SOURMASH_DB/gtdb-rs226.lineages.csv \
    -o sourmash/bins --output-format csv_summary human
cat sourmash/bins.human.txt
```

The lineage is written with the GTDB prefixes: `d__` domain, `p__` phylum, `c__` class, `o__` order, `f__` family, `g__` genus, `s__` species.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
How many bins received a classification? At which rank? Look at the species names: what do names such as `sp002699365` tell you about these organisms?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question" icon=false}
One bin has no match. Does that mean the bin is bad? Compare with its CheckM results before you answer.
:::

The GTDB database is also used by the tool [GTDB-Tk](https://github.com/Ecogenomics/GTDBTk). It uses marker genes and places each genome in a reference tree. It is more sensitive, but its database is far too large for a laptop.

::: {.callout-note title="Optional"}
Run GTDB-Tk on Galaxy: upload your bins to [usegalaxy.eu](https://usegalaxy.eu) and search the tool panel for "GTDB-Tk Classify genomes". Compare its answer with the one of sourmash.
:::
